title: Until They Can't…
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: A middle-school geography teacher of nearly two decades reports on the first fully transfer-focused assessment of his career, given at the close of a Life in the Sahara and Sahel case study. The test named neither the Sahara nor the Sahel; every item put students in an unfamiliar situation and asked them to apply what they had learned elsewhere. The class averaged 96 percent, but the author insists the score matters less than the instructional sequence that produced it. He walks through that sequence in two movements: effortful, spaced and interleaved retrieval until the underlying knowledge is secure in long-term memory, then explicit modeling and heavily varied guided practice of four transferable patterns of environmental adaptation until students cannot help seeing the pattern beneath a new surface. Along the way he credits the researchers who shaped the design, naming Bjork and Bjork on desirable difficulties, Willingham on knowledge and thinking, Ruiz Martin on context variation, Sweller on cognitive load and expertise reversal, and Rosenshine for translating all of it into classroom moves. The closing argument is deliberately unglamorous: transfer does not require reinventing instruction, only building substantial knowledge, making it durable, modeling the thinking, varying the practice conditions, and then handing students a context they have never seen.
points: The assessment is the argument here: by deleting the original context entirely, the author turns transfer from a hoped-for side effect into the thing actually being measured.
Retrieval is framed as a storage-strengthening tool rather than a review activity, with the conditions of retrieval deliberately changed so the knowledge travels when the surface features change.

Four named patterns of adaptation, Chase the Resource, Build a Barrier, Re-Engineer the Land and Hedge Your Bets, act as the portable structure that lets students organize specific examples and then recognize them elsewhere.
The author explicitly rejects discovery: the expert thinking involved in spotting a pattern is modeled aloud first, then practiced with scaffolds that are removed as expertise grows.
He treats the research literature as a set of conditions rather than a script, arguing that principles only become instruction once they meet real students, misconceptions and constraints.
quotes: All of my assessments have asked students to demonstrate what they learned under conditions that were at least somewhat similar to the conditions if not the exact same conditions in which they learned it.

It was the first entirely transfer-focused assessment I have given in my teaching career. There were no questions that asked students to recall something specific about the Sahara or Sahel. In fact, the words Sahara and Sahel do not appear in the assessment.

Transfer cannot begin with an empty long-term memory. Students need sufficient knowledge stored in long-term memory that they can retrieve it when the original scenarios, examples, conditions, and conditions are gone.

They needed to reconstruct knowledge from memory rather than merely see it again. They needed to encounter the same ideas across time and under different conditions so that the knowledge became increasingly secure and flexible when they needed it.
I did not expect students to simply discover how to use those patterns on their own. I explicitly modeled the thinking involved in recognizing them.
Our case study centered on four broad underlying transferable patterns of environmental adaptation: Chase the Resource, Build a Barrier, Re-Engineer the Land, and Hedge Your Bets.

We don't need to reinvent instruction to promote transfer. We need to pay attention to what the evidence tells us about how people learn, the conditions which prompt transfer, and then design instruction with that evidence informing it.
